GoLEBY Research School of Earth Sciences, Australian National University, Canberra A.C.T., Australia (Received February 25, 1980 ; Revised April 30, 1980) The palaeomagnetism of 22 formations from the Cowra Trough and Molong High of South East Australia have been studied. Samples of Ordovician through Middle Devonian age were collected in three major areas, covering a time period crucial to the understanding of the Palaeozoic apparent polar wander path of Australia. Five magnetic components have been identified: 1) A recent field overprint, 2) a secondary component related to the break up of Australia and Antarctica, 3) a predominent Devonian secondary overprint associated with the major orogenic episode, 4) a weak Silurian overprint associated with an earlier orogenic episode, and 5) primary magnetic components ranging in age from the Ordovician to the Devonian. The directions obtained enable construction of a well defined polar wander path for South East Australia and Australia as a whole. 1. Introduction Since the work of LUCK (1973) on the Early Palaeozoic of South East Australia, there have been three interpretations of the available pole positions for Australia. GOLEBY north-south trending tectonic provinces, two of which are the Molong High and Cowra Trough (Fig. 2). The Molong High is dominantly Ordovician, with localized areas of Silurian and Devonian. The Ordovician sequences represent three episodes of tectonic activity: initial andesitic volcanism during the Early Ordovician, followed by a quiet period enabling the deposition of limestones, siltstones, and arenites during the Middle-Late Ordovician. This was followed by a further period of volcanic activity resulting in volcanic tuffs and lavas. Samples were collected stratigraphically through this sequence, and where possible, in the overlying Siluro-Devonian. The Cowra Trough (Fig. 2) formed as a result of internal rifting within the Molong High during the Late Ordovician (SCHEIBNER, 1973). It is dominantly Silurian in age, with isolated areas extending into the Middle Devonian. GOLEBY north-south trending tectonic provinces, two of which are the Molong High and Cowra Trough (Fig. 2). The Molong High is dominantly Ordovician, with localized areas of Silurian and Devonian. The Ordovician sequences represent three episodes of tectonic activity: initial andesitic volcanism during the Early Ordovician, followed by a quiet period enabling the deposition of limestones, siltstones, and arenites during the Middle-Late Ordovician. This was followed by a further period of volcanic activity resulting in volcanic tuffs and lavas. Samples were collected stratigraphically through this sequence, and where possible, in the overlying Siluro-Devonian. The Cowra Trough (Fig. 2) formed as a result of internal rifting within the Molong High during the Late Ordovician (SCHEIBNER, 1973). It is dominantly Silurian in age, with isolated areas extending into the Middle Devonian. GOLEBY north-south trending tectonic provinces, two of which are the Molong High and Cowra Trough (Fig. 2). The Molong High is dominantly Ordovician, with localized areas of Silurian and Devonian. The Ordovician sequences represent three episodes of tectonic activity: initial andesitic volcanism during the Early Ordovician, followed by a quiet period enabling the deposition of limestones, siltstones, and arenites during the Middle-Late Ordovician. This was followed by a further period of volcanic activity resulting in volcanic tuffs and lavas. Samples were collected stratigraphically through this sequence, and where possible, in the overlying Siluro-Devonian. The Cowra Trough (Fig. 2) formed as a result of internal rifting within the Molong High during the Late Ordovician (SCHEIBNER, 1973). It is dominantly Silurian in age, with isolated areas extending into the Middle Devonian. From the remaining Ordovician Formations a primary component and up to four secondary overprint directions were isolated. These were identified using ZIJDERVELD's (1967) orthogonal projections and the least squares method of data analysis. GoLEBY Research School of Earth Sciences, Australian National University, Canberra A.C.T., Australia (Received February 25, 1980 ; Revised April 30, 1980) The palaeomagnetism of 22 formations from the Cowra Trough and Molong High of South East Australia have been studied. Samples of Ordovician through Middle Devonian age were collected in three major areas, covering a time period crucial to the understanding of the Palaeozoic apparent polar wander path of Australia. Five magnetic components have been identified: 1) A recent field overprint, 2) a secondary component related to the break up of Australia and Antarctica, 3) a predominent Devonian secondary overprint associated with the major orogenic episode, 4) a weak Silurian overprint associated with an earlier orogenic episode, and 5) primary magnetic components ranging in age from the Ordovician to the Devonian. The directions obtained enable construction of a well defined polar wander path for South East Australia and Australia as a whole. 1. (1974) proposed a two plate tectonic model based on a difference of 90 degrees in the apparent pole path for the South Eastern part of the Tasman Geosyncline (as defined by PACKHAM, 1969) compared with the simplest interpretation of the pole path for the stable central Australian craton (Fig. 1A). Poles SV, MP, AV, and BG represent the Siluro-Devonian track of South East Australian sub-plate. Since the Late Devonian, the sub-plate was welded to the main craton producing a common track for the whole of Australia. SCHMIDT and MORRIS (1977), by reversing the polarity of the Cambro-Ordovician poles constructed a single apparent polar wander path using all the polar data (Fig. 1B). Two strong points are in favour, l) all the reliable Australian poles are used, and fit stratigraphically in sequence. 2) The angular distance between the Ordovician and the Silurian sections requires less than 90 degrees movement. WILLIAMS Department of Geological Sciences, University of California, Santa Barbara, California 93106 Paleomagnetic results from Miocene flows from the Truk Islands reveal stable magnetization having a declination of +2° and an inclina- tion of +6°, with an ci of 6.8 and a k of 45.4. This is different from the 95 present dipole field at the 95% confidence level. Ten sites are included in the analysis so that major departures from the true mean field direction due to secular variation should have been eliminated. e true mean field direction due to secular variation should have been eliminated. The result gives an ancient latitude of 3°N with a ±3° confidence interval, which is consis- tent with proposed rotation about the Hawaiian hot spot pole at a rate of 1.3 /10 years for the past 10 million years. The directions of magnet- 0 6 ization of flows of Eocene and Miocene age from Saipan reveal a mean direction of magnetization rotated clockwise from the present field direc- tion. Although there are fewer results available from Saipan than from Truk, the results appear to be recording some tectonic rotation and not simply secular variation. The Marianas limestone of Pleistocene age has a direction of magnetization concordant with the present field. These re- sults from Truk and Saipan reveal that tectonic models can indeed be tested in island arc and oceanic island environments by paleomagnetic observations. It is also clear that the paleomagnetism of such islands suf- fers from inadequate numbers of available sites and difficulties in estab- lishing tectonic control. The similarity of the rotation observed at Saipan and Guam strongly suggests that tectonic models of the Marianas must account for major rotation of the southern end of the Marianas since their formation. WILLIAMS Department of Geological Sciences, University of California, Santa Barbara, California 93106 Paleomagnetic results from Miocene flows from the Truk Islands reveal stable magnetization having a declination of +2° and an inclina- tion of +6°, with an ci of 6.8 and a k of 45.4. This is different from the 95 present dipole field at the 95% confidence level. Ten sites are included in the analysis so that major departures from the true mean field direction due to secular variation should have been eliminated. e true mean field direction due to secular variation should have been eliminated. The result gives an ancient latitude of 3°N with a ±3° confidence interval, which is consis- tent with proposed rotation about the Hawaiian hot spot pole at a rate of 1.3 /10 years for the past 10 million years. The directions of magnet- 0 6 ization of flows of Eocene and Miocene age from Saipan reveal a mean direction of magnetization rotated clockwise from the present field direc- tion. Although there are fewer results available from Saipan than from Truk, the results appear to be recording some tectonic rotation and not simply secular variation. The Marianas limestone of Pleistocene age has a direction of magnetization concordant with the present field. These re- sults from Truk and Saipan reveal that tectonic models can indeed be tested in island arc and oceanic island environments by paleomagnetic observations. It is also clear that the paleomagnetism of such islands suf- fers from inadequate numbers of available sites and difficulties in estab- lishing tectonic control. The similarity of the rotation observed at Saipan and Guam strongly suggests that tectonic models of the Marianas must account for major rotation of the southern end of the Marianas since their formation. Member 4 consists of gray and pale gray argillaceous-laminated limestones, bioclastic limestones, and oolitic limestones. Member 5 is composed of purplish red calcareous mudstones with intercalated argillaceous limestones. Conformably overlying these units are the Lower Triassic Maocaopu Formation and the Middle Triassic Songzikan Formation, both consisting mainly of dolomites and limestones deposited in a marine environment, which are in turn, disconformably overlain by Upper Triassic quartzose sandstones, shales, and siltstones with coal seams (Xujiahe Formation). The Lower Triassic sediments vary lithologically on a regional basis, from west to east, changing from a proximal clastic facies (Feixiaguan Formation) through a mixed facies of clastics and carbonates (Yelang Formation) to a carbonate marine facies (Daye Formation) (Yang Zunyi et al., 1982). The sampling area is in the transitional facies zone of mixed clastics and limestone. For this reason the Yelang Formation at the northwest limb is thicker and with more clastic beds. Flint SUMMARY: The Coloso Formation is an early Cretaceous conglomerate-dominated molasse sequence in northern Chile. The sequence was deposited rapidly and records the unroofing of granodioritic and andesitic source rocks. Thin sand units throughout the sequence have been studied palaeomagnetically; the results are complex but can be related to the diagenesis of and-zone alluvium. Natural remanent magnetization (NRM) may be normal or reversed but is usually a combination of the two. Isolation of magnetic components by vector analysis of thermal and AF demagnetization data yields both normal and reversed components which are approximately antiparallel and yield an average pole position at 703, 192"E. This is consistent with late Cretaceous data from northern Chile but not with the established apparent polar wander (APW) path for South America. It may indicate late Cretaceous remagnetization but is considered to be more likely an indication that the present APW path assumes no tectonic rotation and that important relative movements have taken place between northern Chile and Argentina. Samples of this type are not considered fundamentally different from those which show N + R components in both AF and thermally demagnetized specimens. carrier_identity_candidates.excerpt: e fan bodies which prograded towards the NE. They pass laterally into an upper conglomerate sequence, and together these comprise the Lombriz Formation. The Lombriz Formation is overlain by shallow-marine Neocomian limestones of the Tableado Formation (formerly the Way Formation). Diagenetic studies of the orebody and associated sediments reveal a number of features characteristic of the shallow burial diagenesis of arid-zone continental sediments (Walker et al. 1978; Turner 1980). These include dissolution and clay replacement of detrital silicate grains and a suite of authigenic minerals including quartz, feldspar, calcite and hematite. In shallow burial diagenesis, reaction between detrital grains and groundwater controls the supply of ions to interstitial pore solutions. n the central Andes (Coloso Formation, Northern Chile) P. Turner, H. Clemmey & S. Flint SUMMARY: The Coloso Formation is an early Cretaceous conglomerate-dominated molasse sequence in northern Chile. The sequence was deposited rapidly and records the unroofing of granodioritic and andesitic source rocks. Thin sand units throughout the sequence have been studied palaeomagnetically; the results are complex but can be related to the diagenesis of and-zone alluvium. Natural remanent magnetization (NRM) may be normal or reversed but is usually a combination of the two. Isolation of magnetic components by vector analysis of thermal and AF demagnetization data yields both normal and reversed components which are approximately antiparallel and yield an average pole position at 703, 192"E. This is consistent with late Cretaceous data from northern Chile but not with the established apparent polar wander (APW) path for South America. It may indicate late Cretaceous remagnetization but is considered to be more likely an indication that the present APW path assumes no tectonic rotation and that important relative movements have taken place between northern Chile and Argentina. WATTS Department of Geology, The University, Glasgow, G12 8QQ, U.K. (Received 23 August 1984; accepted 1 February 1985) Abstract - Palaeomagnetic data from mid to late Palaeozoic rocks are potentially valuable for testing models of the assembly of Spitsbergen and for determining the palaeo-position of parts of Spitsbergen relative to the major tectonic elements that comprised the Old Red Continent. Fine-grained red sandstones from the Tournaisian to Namurian Billefjorden Group, collected by members of Cambridge Spitsbergen expeditions, were subjected to stepwise chemical and thermal demagnetization. The characteristic magnetization is found in normal and reverse polarities and corresponds to a pole position at 23° S, 332 °E, dp = 5.7°, dm = 10.5°, which is near an early Carboniferous pole computed for the Baltic Shield-Russian Platform (Baltica). When compared to Laurentia (North America) in the context of the revised Mauch Chunk palaeomagnetic study, Spitsbergen falls a few degrees south of the Bullard reconstruction but the error of the determination of the palaeolatitude overlaps with this position. Therefore relative motion between any part of Spitsbergen and Laurentia and Baltica during the Carboniferous is not resolved. 1. Introd

The elements are Laurentia (North America with the Labrador Sea closed), Baltica (Baltic Shield with the Russian Platform) and Armorica (southern Europe). According to this hypothesis, the three elements were joined during Old Red Sandstone time (late Silurian to late Devonian) but Baltica and Armorica were 15° to 20° south of the Bullard, Everett & Smith (1965) position. Baltica and Armorica then moved northward with respect to North America to the Bullard, Everett & Smith (1965) position during early Carboniferous time along strike slip faults. The driving force of this movement, was-the collision of Gondwanaland with the Old Red Continent. Slivers of continental crust with dimensions of the order of several hundred kilometres that were on the European side of the strike slip lineament(s) but remained attached to North America after the opening of the present Atlantic Ocean are now identified as displaced terrains such as Acadia (Kent & Opdyke, 1978). Introduction The mid to late Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic record of the Atlantic-bordering continents may be used to determine the disposition of the tectonic elements related to the later stages of evolution of the Caledonian-Appalachian mountain belts. Of recent interest is the documentation of the extent and movement of displaced terrains within this belt (Kent & Opdyke, 1978, 1979; Van der Voo, French & French, 1979) and, on the larger scale, possible departure of the distribution of the major continental areas from the Bullard, Everett & Smith (1965) and similar reconstructions (Scotese et al. 1979; Van der Voo, 1983). Lefort & Van der Voo (1981) and Van der Voo (1983) outlined a testable hypothesis, based on available palaeomagnetic data, of the disposition of three major tectonic elements that comprised the Old Red Continent. The elements are Laurentia (North America with the Labrador Sea closed), Baltica (Baltic Shield with the Russian Platform) and Armorica (southern Europe). According to this hypoth

Baltica and Armorica then moved northward with respect to North America to the Bullard, Everett & Smith (1965) position during early Carboniferous time along strike slip faults. The driving force of this movement, was-the collision of Gondwanaland with the Old Red Continent. Slivers of continental crust with dimensions of the order of several hundred kilometres that were on the European side of the strike slip lineament(s) but remained attached to North America after the opening of the present Atlantic Ocean are now identified as displaced terrains such as Acadia (Kent & Opdyke, 1978). As argued by Harland (1978), Harland & Wright (1979), and Harland (1980), the idea of sinistral strike slip motion displacing slivers of continental crust during the late stages of the Caledonian orogeny is an attractive hypothesis that explains many aspects of the geology of Spitsbergen. Spitsbergen may be divided into at least three provinces of older rocks which are separated by two major fault zones. The eastern province has strong similarities to central eastern Greenland (Harland, 1978; Harland & Wright, 1979). Cervid teeth are very similar to giraffid teeth; it is possible that some of the dentitions identified in our faunal list as giraffids may prove to be cervid and conversely, some of the teeth identified as cervids in the earlier faunal lists may prove to be giraffids. Definite identification of the dentitions must await a more detailed taxonomic review of all Siwalik Giraffidae and Cervidae. Until then, we are aware of no antlers recorded from the Tatrot section (or elsewhere in Middle Siwalik deposits), whereas antlers and crania with antlers are fairly common in Upper Siwalik deposits. Lydekker's Cervus latidens, based on a right upper molar, is from the Padhri--Hasnot area where we record several dentitions of giraffids. It should be noted that cervids with antlers (e.g., Procervulus and Stephanocemas) are recorded from Miocene deposits in Europe and northern Asia. rn Asia. The sequence of faunal change in Siwalik sediments is of primary import- ance for the correlation of these terrestrial sediments and related geologic events with similar deposits and events in other parts of the world. Paleontol- ogists and stratigraphers have commonly placed the faunal sequence within a framework established by Pilgrim (1913), relating these divisions (Manchar or Kamlial, Chinji, Nagri, Dhok Pathan, Bhandar, Tatrot, Pinjor, and Boulder Conglomerate) to lithologic formations, or biostratigraphic (zones), or time- stratigraphic (stages) units. It is now apparent that these faunal-stratigraphic divisions are fairly reliable for intercontinental correlation but are unreliable for correlation within the Siwaliks. For example, most paleontologists and stratigraphers accept the correlation of Pilgrim's Pinjor fauna with the European Villafranchian or Biharian fauna, but there is little or no agree- ment on where to place the boundary between Pilgrim's Pinjor and Tatrot faunal intervals in the Siwaliks. For this reason, we have avoided (up to now) placing any sites in Pilgrim's Pinjor or Tatrot faunal intervals, but have placed all of them in an independent, calibrated temporal frame of reference, the geomagnetic time scale. stratigraphy and vertebrate paleontology of the Upper Siwalik subgroup of northern Pakistan. Palaeogeogr., Palaeoclimatol., Palaeoecol., 27 : 1--34. Two hundred and fifty three sites consisting of three samples per site were taken from eight separate stratigraphic sections from sediments of the Upper Siwalik subgroup of northern Pakistan. All samples have been partially demagnetized in alternating fields of from 150 to 300 Oe. The sediments are dipping at angles of up to 75 ° in a variety of directions, and the locality mean directions improve significantly after correcting for bedding attitude, providing a statistically significant fold test at the 95% level. The magnetic stratigraphy was obtained based on the statistically significant well- grouped partially demagnetized data. Two prominent bentonitized tufts occur in several sections above and below a prominent reversal of the earth's magnetic field. Radiometric dates of 2.3 + 0.4 m.y.B.P, and 2.5 + 0.4 m.y.B.P, have been obtained by fission track on zircons from these tufts. This allows the magnetic stratigraphy to be correlated to the standard reversal chronology of the Pliocene and Pleistocene. The longest stratigraphic section (1.87 km in thickness) can be shown to span the time between 0.6 m.y.B.P, and 5.5 m.y.B.P

Magnetic polarity stratigraphy and vertebrate paleontology of the Upper Siwalik subgroup of northern Pakistan. Palaeogeogr., Palaeoclimatol., Palaeoecol., 27 : 1--34. Two hundred and fifty three sites consisting of three samples per site were taken from eight separate stratigraphic sections from sediments of the Upper Siwalik subgroup of northern Pakistan. All samples have been partially demagnetized in alternating fields of from 150 to 300 Oe. The sediments are dipping at angles of up to 75 ° in a variety of directions, and the locality mean directions improve significantly after correcting for bedding attitude, providing a statistically significant fold test at the 95% level. The magnetic stratigraphy was obtained based on the statistically significant well- grouped partially demagnetized data. Two prominent bentonitized tufts occur in several sections ab

four meters per thousand years for the Rohtas anticline and three meters per thousand years for the Pabhi Hills. The rates of subsidence (i.e., rates of sedimentation) of the various sections are estimated to range from 0.35 m/103 yr to 0.50 m/103 yr. The first occurrence of conglomerate-containing clasts derived from the Himalayan uplift occurs just prior to the Olduvai event at the base of the Pleistocene. INTRODUC~ON The result of the collision of the Indian Plate with the Eurasian continent can be seen today in the awe-inspiring Himalayan mountain chain. This orogeny is in part recorded in the sediments derived from them and deposited to the south of the mountains in a subsiding foredeep. These sediments, the Neogene and Quaternary Siwalik Group, contain the remains of the vertebrate faunas which lived on the Indian plate during the late Cenozoic. These faunas have been extensively collected and are well-known as the standard land mammal stages of southern Asia. The Siwalik Group has in turn become involved in the continuing orogeny and has become faulted and folded and is now under active erosion, leading to an abundance of excellent exposures available for study. The sites were taken from the Chinji, Nagri, Dhok Pathan and Upper Siwalik formations which span the last 14 m.y. of Earth history. The formations have been deformed in the ongoing Himalayan orogeny and are exposed today in sections which dip at angles of from 10 ° to 90 ° in different directions. A characteristic direction of magnetization was isolated at all sections by thermal demagnetization at temperatures of from 550 ° to 650°C. The sediments have been folded within the last 2 m.y. and because of a positive fold test it can be shown that the characteristic magnetization of these sediments was acquired before folding. Four of the sections have directions of magnetization which have been rotated in a counter-clockwise fashion up to 40 ° ; however, sections taken along the Indus River, the north flank of the Soan syncline and the south flank of the Salt Range show small counter-clockwise rota- tions of under 10 ° . These observations are in agreement with previous suggestions that strata in the Salt Range have been moved to the south and rotated in a counter-clockwise fashion. Paleomagnetism of the Middle Siwalik formations of northern Pakistan and rota- tion of the Salt Range Decollement. Palaeogeogr., Palaeoclimatol., Palaeoecol., 37: 1--15. Sampling for paleomagnetic study has been carried out at seven localities in the Potwar Plateau region of Pakistan in the vicinity of the Salt Range. In all, 253 sites, consisting of three samples per site, were studied. The sites were taken from the Chinji, Nagri, Dhok Pathan and Upper Siwalik formations which span the last 14 m.y. of Earth history. The formations have been deformed in the ongoing Himalayan orogeny and are exposed today in sections which dip at angles of from 10 ° to 90 ° in different directions. A characteristic direction of magnetization was isolated at all sections by thermal demagnetization at temperatures of from 550 ° to 650°C. section_candidates.excerpt: racteristic magnetization of these sediments was acquired before folding. Four of the sections have directions of magnetization which have been rotated in a counter-clockwise fashion up to 40 ° ; however, sections taken along the Indus River, the north flank of the Soan syncline and the south flank of the Salt Range show small counter-clockwise rota- tions of under 10 ° . These observations are in agreement with previous suggestions that strata in the Salt Range have been moved to the south and rotated in a counter-clockwise fashion. The observations reported here indicate that the paleomagnetic poles derived from Cambrian and Permian formations within the Salt Range have probably also suffered rotation and should be removed from consideration in Gondwanaland reconstruction of the Paleozoic. In the initial studies on the sediments reported here, a.f. demagnetization was also attempted. It soon became apparent, however, that in these red colored sediments, a.f. demagnetization was inadequate to remove secondary components of magnetization since in these older forma- tions much of the remanence is carried by hematite (Tauxe, 1979; Tauxe et al., 1980). Washakie Basin, Wyoming The Eocene, fluviatile to lacustrine Washakie Formation is the youngest early Tertiary rock unit cropping out in the Washakie Basin of southwestern 343 Wyoming. The Washakie Basin is a synclinal, structural and topographic basin covering an area of approximately 2500 square miles (6500 square kilometers; Roehler, 1973). It is flanked by the Sierra Madre Range to the east, Wamsutter Arch to the north, Rock Springs Uplift to the west, and Cherokee Ridge to the south. Eocene strata in the basin are approximately 8000 ft {2438 m) thick. Surface sections of the Washakie Formation yield a maximum thickness of approximately 3000 ft (914 m), although Roehler (1969) indicated a possible subsurface thickness of 12,300 ft (3749 m) for the formation. Roehler (1973) divided the Washakie Formation into a lower Kinney Rim Member and an upper Adobe Town Member. Investigation of the biostratigraphy, magnetostrati- graphy and radioisotopic chronology of Eocene sequences in Wyoming and California may greatly increase the temporal precision of intracontinental correlations. A multidisciplinary approach is extremely useful in solving problems in paleontology, geology, and other aspects of earth history. A broad perspective and diverse sources of data often contribute information and in- sights essential to the resolution of scientific inquiries. In this study I attempt to integrate marine and continental biostratigraphy, magnetic polarity stratigraphy, and radioisotopic chronology in a synthetic correlation of sedimentary sequences from the western United States. A few detailed, multi- disciplinary correlation studies have been attempted for late Tertiary deposits, but similar projects have rarely been undertaken for the early Tertiary. This study emphasizes original paleomagnetic analyses of strata containing approximately equivalent mammalian faunas, and at least one other source of temporal data. Washakie Basin, Wyoming The Eocene, fluviatile to lacustrine Washakie Formation is the youngest early Tertiary rock unit cropping out in the Washakie Basin of southwestern 343 Wyoming. The Washakie Basin is a synclinal, structural and topographic basin covering an area of approximately 2500 square miles (6500 square kilometers; Roehler, 1973). It is flanked by the Sierra Madre Range to the east, Wamsutter Arch to the north, Rock Springs Uplift to the west, and Cherokee Ridge to the south. Eocene strata in the basin are approximately 8000 ft {2438 m) thick. Surface sections of the Washakie Formation yield a maximum thickness of approximately 3000 ft (914 m), although Roehler (1969) indicated a possible subsurface thickness of 12,300 ft (3749 m) for the formation. Roehler (1973) divided the Washakie Formation into a lower Kinney Rim Member and an upper Adobe Town Member. At its type section the Kinney Rim Member (Beds 515--568) is 893.9 ft thick (272.5 m; Roehler, 1973). A complete section for the Adobe Town Member (Beds 569--708)

The faunal succession of this deposit indicates an age ranging from middle Paleocene (Torrejonian) to early Eocene (Clarkforkian). A minimum of three separately oriented paleomagnetic samples were collected from each of 53 sites in the type and one reference section. Depending upon pilot studies and lithology, in the laboratory the paleomagnetic specimens were treated with either AF or thermal demagnetization (at, respectively, a minimum regime of 25 mT or 200° and 400°C), which appeared to isolate the characteristic component of magnetization. The magnetic polarity zonation is predominantly reversed punctuated by several normal intervals. Based on the faunal constraints and magnetostratigraphic pattern, the Black Peaks is correlated to the reversed zone below chron 26, to the base of chron 24, or an absolute interval of time ranging from about 62 to 53 Ma. Black Peaks Formation consists of fluviatile mudstones, silts, and sands. The faunal succession of this deposit indicates an age ranging from middle Paleocene (Torrejonian) to early Eocene (Clarkforkian). A minimum of three separately oriented paleomagnetic samples were collected from each of 53 sites in the type and one reference section. Depending upon pilot studies and lithology, in the laboratory the paleomagnetic specimens were treated with either AF or thermal demagnetization (at, respectively, a minimum regime of 25 mT or 200° and 400°C), which appeared to isolate the characteristic component of magnetization. The magnetic polarity zonation is predominantly reversed punctuated by several normal intervals. Based on the faunal constraints and magnetostratigraphic pattern, the Black Peaks is correlated to the reversed zone below chron 26, to the base of chron 24, or an absolute interval of time ranging from about 62 to 53 Ma. Previous hypotheses that the Javelina-Black Peaks and Black Peaks-Hannold Hill lithological boundaries approximate, respectively, the Cretaceous-Paleocene and Paleocene-Eocene boundaries, need to be revised in light of the present study. INTRODUCTION The Black Peaks Formation of Big Bend National Park, Texas, consists of continental sedimentary deposits containing several sig- nificant Paleocene and early Eocene faunas. The geologic history of this formation is im- portant because it is the only Paleocene sedimentary rock unit found in the Trans- Pecos region, and it also contains the south- ernmost occurrence of large Paleocene mam- malian faunas so far discovered in North America (Schiebout 1974, 1980). The purpose of this report is to present the chronology of the Black Peaks Formation by the establish- ment of a magnetic polarity stratigraphy for this unit. On a broader scale, comparisons will then be made with other roughly contem- poraneous faunas which will provide a better understanding of early Tertiary biostratig- raphy and paleobiogeography. 1 Manuscript received November 18, 1982; re- vised May 13, 1983. 2 Present address: Core Labs, 7501 Stemmons Frwy., Box 47547, Dallas, TX 75247. The sequence represents (from oldest to youngest) the Chiquimil A, Araucanense, and Corral Quemado Formations. Paleomagnetic samples were collected from 99 stratigraphic levels. Strong-field thermomagnetic and isothermal remanent magnetization experiments indicate that the dominant ferrimagnetic mineral is magnetite. Progressive alternating-field (AF) and themal demagnetization of the natural remanent magnetism (NRM) demonstrates that AF demagnetization to 20 mT peak field is sufficient to isolate the primary NRM which is of depositional origin. The resulting paleomagnetic data provide a well-defined magnetic polarity zonation, although sampling is less dense in the upper half of the section. 40K -40Ar data obtained from mineral separates of four tuffs within the section allow reliable age determinations for those levels. INTRODUCTION The continents of North and South America are today connected by the Panama- nian land bridge, a structure which has per- mitted the reciprocal interchange of terres- trial biotas following its final emergence about 3.0 Ma. This biotic event is known as the Great American Faunal Interchange (Webb 1976), and it represents the best docu- mented example in the fossil record of an in- terchange

Second-order events such as these may reflect major, long-sustained shifts in local hydrologic regimen or changes in source area provenance. Schumm (1977, p. 330) defines third-order fluvial cycles as those related to geomorphic thresholds, or step-functions. A definitive cri- teria for a third-order fluvial cycle is the de- velopment of channeling in fluvial deposits. The channel sand/overbank couplet that Allen (1965) defines as the basic fluvial cycle unit would thus be third-order. In the Siwalik sys- tem such third-order fluvial cycles have a 104-105 years periodicity. Lastly, Schumm (1977, p. 330) cites storm and seasonal events as the cause of fourth- order fluvial cycles. In the overbank deposits of the Siwaliks system stratified clays, silts, and sands are frequently intermixed with paleosol horizons. These deposits are gener- ally attributed to seasonal or flood events, which would qualify them as fourth-order fluvial cycles. In the Siwalik system such fourth-order cycles would have return pe- riods spanning a wide range, probably 10°- 104 years depending on the space scale and the process involved. SEDIMENTARY PETROLOGY

In addition, theoretical and experimental evaluations of the effects of shock on rema- nent magnetization have been reported by Hargraves and Perkins (1969), Nagata (1971), Pohl et al. (1975), and Cisowski and Fuller (1978). These studies confirm that shock waves with an amplitude of a few GPa are sufficient to impart a magnetization to rocks with a significant content of low- to moder- ate-coercivity magnetite. A majority of these studies dealt with igneous rocks, and only one (Cisowski and Fuller 1978) reported re- sults on sedimentary carbonates. Kaibab Limestone samples from Barringer Crater contained a pre-deformational overprinted magnetization, which Cisowski and Fuller (1978) concluded was a SRM. Cisowski and Fuller (1978) found that the range of unblocking temperatures (Tub'S) of an experimentally-induced SRM extended beyond 500°C. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: uller (1978) found that the range of unblocking temperatures (Tub'S) of an experimentally-induced SRM extended beyond 500°C. The shock magnetization pro- cess thus appears to be controlled by the coercivity of the magnetite grains present, af- fecting only the low-coercivity fraction, but partially activating the entire Tub spectrum. However, because Tub's depend upon coer- civity as well as upon grain volume and time (Neel 1955), most of the SRM also resides in the low Tub fraction and is therefore vulner- able to thermal perturbations. Thermal reset- ting of magnetic remanence at low to moder- ate temperatures (well below the Curie temperature) depends strongly on the time available for the magnetization to equilibrate with an ambient field. In natural events (im- pact or otherwise) where large volumes of rock are heated by shock, cooling proceeds slowly, and time may be available for significant thermal resetting of the SRM. In naturally shocked rocks which have attained moderate temperatures, one might expect any acquired SRM to be overprinted signif- icantly by a post-deformational partial TRM in the low Tub range, while any surviving SRM will reside in grains with higher Tub'S. Varne & Rubenach (1972) argue from petrological evi- dence that the island rocks are similar to those formed at accreting plate margins. The structure of Macquarie Island is far more complex; the island rocks are heavily faulted and steep, variable dips are observed for the dolerite dykes, and for the layering in the pillow lavas. Nonetheless, in many localities the strikes of lava flows approximately parallel the strikes of the dykes that cut them, and on this evidence Varne & Rubenach (1972) argue that tilting has often occurred about horizontal axes roughly parallel to the strike of the dykes. The predominant strike of the dykes is approxi- mately eastnortheast parallel to the regional strike of seafloor-spreading magnetic anomalies as interpreted by Williamson (1974). COLLECTION OF SAMPLES Eighty-six oriented block samples were collected from 32 sites (Fig. 3). Twenty of these sites were located in individual dolerite dykes, nine in basaltic lava flows, and one in each of serpentinite, gabbro, and red sediment. Because of the normally overcast weather conditions, samples were oriented using a com- pass and inclinometer. Although the compass bearing was not visibly effected by the mag- netism of the rock outcrops, small errors in compass bearing may have resulted. DISCUSSION The effectiveness of the two corrections used in this study is consistent with the implied model for the generation of ocean crust. The success of the bedding correction in reducing the 95 percent confidence radius from 25° to 12° argues that the lavas were laid roughly horizontally and the dykes injected roughly vertically. The success of the rotation correc- tion on the directions from block 3 which brought the palaeomagnetic poles from blocks 2 and 3 into statistical agreement, also argues that dykes are injected roughly parallel to the spreading centre (and to the consequent sea- floor-spreading anomalies). The residual dispersion on the directions of magnetization after correction could be the result of the lavas' being laid down subhori- zontally and the dykes being injected sub- vertically and subparallel to the spreading centre. WILLIAMSON (With 3 Tables and 6 Figures) (MS received 8 August 1978) ABSTRACT Macquarie Island offers a rare opportunity to investigate outcropping ocean crust. In this study, palaeomagnetic samples were collected from 32 sites. After frequency demagnetization, 15 of these sites were found to be stable. Stable sites were from lavas, dykes, and gabbros, representing different depths of formation in the oceanic crust. A successful bedding correction, assuming a simple model for the oceanic crust, was applied to the directions of magnetization. The former assumed dykes were injected vertically, lavas laid down horizontally, and gabbros layered horizontally. However, the palaeomagnetic poles from the centre and south of the island were not conformable at their 95 percent confidence levels. However, the palaeomagnetic poles from the centre and south of the island were not conformable at their 95 percent confidence levels. To remedy this, a structural correction was then applied to sites from the south of the island, where the average strike of dykes is 55° different from that in the centre of the island, which parallels regional seafloor-spreading anomalies. This correction involved rotation around a vertical axis, which could not be accounted for in a simple bedding correction. When the average strike of the dykes was brought into parallelism with that of the regional seafloor-spreading anomalies (and presumably that of the fossil spreading ridge), the result was to bring the palaeomagnetic poles from the centre and the south of the island into conformity. The final pole for Macquarie Island was found to be consistent with a pole of similar age from the Australian Continent. Cubic specimens (15 mm edges) were cut from the samples and subjected to a modified Thellier procedure (Thellier & Thellier, 1959; Nagata et al., 1963; Coe, 1967a). Laboratory heatings were carried out in a furnace at a series of progressively higher temperatures between 140°C and 680°C. Specimens were heated twice to each temperature, cooled and remeasured; the first of each pair of heatings was conducted in zero magnetic field (achieved with a surrounding coil system; McElhinny et al., 1971), and the second in the ambient laboratory magnetic field (60 <"T). The first heating and cooling cycle removes a portion of the natural remanent magnetisation (NRM), and the second replaces it with a laboratory thermoremanent magnetisation (TRM). Since TRM is proportional to the magnetic field in which it is acquired, com- parisons between the NRM and laboratory TRM pro- vide estimates of ancient geomagnetic field strength. In practice, however, the points are scattered by experimental error, weathering, changes in the magnetic minerals during the laboratory heat- ings, and other forms of non-ideal behaviour (Coe, 19676). The direction for basalt at Mt Schank differs from that of Mt Gambier by several degrees, and indicates that the two volcanoes differ in age, probably by three centuries or more. Directions for both volcanoes are much shallower than the present-day geomagnetic direction at the locality. Palaeomagnetic field strength estimates, from baked ash at Mt Gambier and baked sand at Mt Schank, are higher than the present-day field strength. Mount Schank rises abruptly from the surrounding plain 14 km south of Mt Gambier (Fig. lb). It is a complex maar-cone structure, where the combina- tion of abundant groundwater and small magma source produced an edifice smaller than Mt Gambier. Initially lava flowed westward from a NW trending line or fissure, marked now by a line of small scoria cones (Fig. 3). More explosive activity followed, with the development of a larger scoria cone and small maar at the southern end of the fissure. A large hybrid maar-cone structure, straddling the small maar and almost obliterating the larger scoria cone, marks the end of activity at Mt Schank (Joyce, 1971; Sheard, 1980). ROBERTSON Department of Physics University of Auckland Private Bag Auckland, New Zealand* Abstract A paleomagnetic study has been made of 99 specimens from 11 sites in the recent basalt lavas of Rangitoto Island. The measured natural remanent magnetisation (NRM) had a formation mean direction of 1.9°E, -62.1°, (X95 = 2.6°; ther­ mal cleaning changed the formation mean NRM direction only slightly to 0.2°E, -61. 7°, Ct9 5 = 1.8°. The densities, magnetisations, and magnetic sus­ ceptibilities measured for each site are recorded. Since Konigsberger's Qn ratio is large in every case, it follows that the aeromagnetic total force anomaly is symmetrical about the geographic meridian. Paleomagnetic declinations, at each site, when compared with historically recorded declinations of the geomagnetic field, confirm the dating results previously obtained by the 14C method; that is, Rangitoto was an active volcano between A.D. 850 and A.D. 1800, with a maximum of activity between A.D. 1200 and A.D. 1500. It is inferred that near Auckland the geomagnetic field has changed direction at approximately 2.87 X 10-2 deg/year eastwards, and changed little in inclina­ tion, during the last 1000 years. A dark, densely welded lenticulite containing large black fiamme is at the base, grading upwards to a grey, densely welded ignimbrite containing randomly oriented black pumice clasts «150 mm) at the top. The basallenticulite is best exposed in a reference section within the Matahana Basin, 2.3 km northeast of the type section (N85/573884). The ignimbrite is generally deficient in crystals; phenocrysts include plagioclase, magnetite, hyper­ sthene, calcium-poor clinopyroxene, and horn­ blende. Quartz is confined to the upper third of the flow. Small rhyolite xenoliths are common. The full extent of the ignimbrite is unknown as much was removed by erosion prior to eruption of the Marshall Ignimbrite, and present outcrop is restricted by the cover of younger pyroclastics and alluvium. However, it does extend south from the Matahana Basin towards the Guthrie Graben where it is presumably downthrown by northwest-trending faults. On Harry Johnson Road (N85/584854) a basalt scoria deposit contains xenoliths of Tikorangi Ignimbrite indicating that it is present at depth in thi

described elsewhere (Murphy 1977). RAHOPAKA IGNIMBRITE (ri) (new name) The type section of the Rahopaka Ignimbrite is a 300 m roadside section extending east from the Pukerimu- Tikorangi Roads junction at N85/546873 to 550874. The ignimbrite is flat lying, 60+ m thick, and overlies pyroclastic deposits. At the type section the lower contact of the Rahopaka Ignimbrite is obscured by a slip, but above this it is grey-brown, crystal rich, and densely welded near the base. The degree of welding decreases towards the top where it is generally only moderately welded. Phenocrysts in decreasing order of abundance are plagioclase, quartz, hornblende, magnetite, and hypersthene. The visible abundance of green-brown hornblende is the most characteristic mineralogical feature of this ignimbrite. The ignimbrite base is also exposed on Rusa Road, 1.8 km from the Tikorangi-Rusa Roads junction (N85/582851) where it is poorly welded and again overlies pyroclastics with a basal 70 mm thick pumice ash zone. In this region the base has a transgressive red colouration, variable in thickness, and attributed to post-depositional oxidation during cooling of the ignimbrite flow. Xenoliths of Rahopaka Ignimbrite in basaltic scoria on Harry Johnson Road (N85/584854) indicate that, like the Tikorangi Ignimbrite, the

nimbrite unconformably overlies the Marshall Ignimbrite and is itself unconformably overlain by the Mamaku Ignimbrite. MAMAKU IGNIMBRITE (mk) This was named by Martin (1961) who defined the type locality as the gorge of the Mangarewa Stream at the Kaharoa- Tauranga Road Bridge (N67/646258). Briggs (1973) gives a generalised profile through the ignimbrite at the type area. It crops out in the southwest of the Matahana Basin where it separates into a number of flows. Here it is a crystal-rich quartzose ignimbrite which, apart from a thin zone of dense welding, is generally poorly welded. Phenocrysts consist of plagioclase, quartz, hypersthene, magnetite, and trace amounts of hornblende. Twelve ignimbrite formations of the Taupo-Rotorua district are all normally magnet­ ised, and are referred to the Brunhes Normal Paleomagnetic Epoch (Cox 1969, 1971), that is, <0.72 Ma (scale of McDougall 1979), while the Waiteariki and Whitianga Ignimbrites, and the Ongatiti Ignimbrite and Rangitoto Ignimbrite Group are all reversely magnetised (Cox 1969, 1971; Kohn 1973). To test the stability of the NRM, at least 1 sample from each site or ignimbrite was partially demagnet­ ised in alternating magnetic fields of 50, 100, 150, 200,250, and 300 oersteds (Oe). A demagnetisation diagram was produced for each sample by plotting the end point of the resultant magnetisation vector after every step (Zijderveld 1967). In all but 1 case, the resultant magnetisation vector decreased towards the centre of the co-ordinate system and showed a stable magnetic component remaining after removal of a weak secondary viscous remanent magnetisation (VRM). In most test samples the VRM was removed by an alternating field of 150 Oe. All samples were then cleaned at 200 Oe. ABSTRACT Lord Howe Island is the eroded remnant of a large shield volcano. Tholeiitic lavas of the North Ridge Basalt comprise the main shield building phase and were erupted about 6.9 Ma ago. The Boat Harbour Breccia probably formed within the throat of the volcano and, together with the North Ridge Basalt, is intruded by numerous basaltic dykes, which grade into a cone sheet complex near the main vent. Large scale collapse of the summit area of the volcano produced a caldera which was filled rapidly by lavas of the Mount Lidgbird Basalt some 6.4 Ma ago, bringing to a close the volcanic history of Lord Howe Island

Virtually no outcrops are found on the higher parts of Intermediate Hill, above about 100 m altitude, but it is inferred from the distribution of outcrops of the breccia that it underlies the whole of this area, as shown on the map (Fig. 3). Nevertheless, a number of massive smooth outcrops of weathered, structureless, basaltic rock that are not breccia occur on the ridge running from Rocky Point toward the summit of Intermediate Hill, especially at an altitude of about 100 m. Similar out- crops are found at an altitude of about 60 to 80 m on the NE slopes of Intermediate Hill above Rocky Run. In thin section these rocks are seen to be exten- sively altered with development of chlorite, epidote and calcite, although clearly originally of basaltic composition. No lava flow tops or bottoms were found, and thus possibly the rocks may be intrusive bodies. The origin of the Boat Harbour Breccia is prob- lematical, but we suggest that it was formed mainly by explosive volcanism within the central vent region of the volcano, and therefore may be an agglomerate. On the northern flanks of Mount Lidgbird the cal- dera margin can be rocated only approximately, owing to lack of outcrop. However, in a prominent buttress on the NW flanks of Mount Lidgbird (Fig. 9), at an elevation of about 150 m, caldera-filling lavas and interbedded conglomerate lap onto a complex of basaltic dykes and fragmental material, possibly erupted along or adjacent to the caldera boundary fault, as at Red Point. Game (1970) has given detailed petrographic de- scriptions of the Mount Lidgbird Basalt, and he pre- sented much data on their chemistry and mineralogy. The basalts range from strongly porphyritic types to almost aphyric types. Moderately phyric lavas are most common with olivine as phenocrysts, but plagio- clase and clinopyroxene occur also. The rocks typi- cally have an intergranular groundmass, commonly exhibiting flow texture, and consisting of plagioclase, clinopyroxene, olivine (commonly iddingsitised), iron oxide and varying proportions (up to 25 percent) of mesostasis, which is poorly crystallised to glassy. The mesostasis is turbid with alteration and is partly re- placed i

also be classified as transitional. Thus the main shield-building lavas (North Ridge Basalt) are tholeiitic basalts, the dykes are olivine basalts, and the caldera-filling lavas (Mount Lidg- bird Basalt) are transitional to alkali olivine basalts and hawaiites. This change in composition with time from tholeiitic to alkaline is commonly observed in oceanic volcanoes, for example in many of the Hawaiian volcanoes (Macdonald & Katsura, 1964) and in Reunion (Upton & Wadsworth, 1972). GEOCHRONOLOGY Methods Samples were collected from many of the lavas and dykes for possible potassium-argon (K-Ar) age deter- mination. Each sample was examined in thin section, but very few were holocrystalline and free of altera- tion. Nevertheless, some samples met the minimum criteria for dating as whole rocks. Each sample was crushed to a fragment size of —1 mm + 0.5 mm, an aliquant was taken and crushed to less than 0.15 mm, and this representative sample was reserved for potas- sium analysis by flame photometry. Laboratory procedures for measurement of the direction of magnetisation are similar to those de- scribed previously (McElhinny, 1973). Alternating field (AF) demagnetisation procedures were used on all samples, and in some cases thermal demagnetisa- tion was undertaken; these techniques were employed to investigate the stability spectra of the magnetisa- tion components. Dykes and sheets Oriented samples were collected from each of 32 dykes and sheets, well-distributed through the North Ridge Basalt in the northern half of the island and in the Boat Harbour Breccia. Seven of the sites were in basaltic sheets (dips < 45°) on the western shores of Boat Harbour; although the sheets are considered to be just dykes with a shallower dip, results from them will be considered separately, at least initially. With few exceptions, samples from individual intru- sives yielded well-grouped directions subsequent to AF demagnetisation (Table 4). Only at one site does the within-site scatter exceed 18° at the 95 percent confidence level. Twenty-eight of the sites show reversed polarity and the other four have normal polarity, three of which are from North Ridge and the fourth from Rabbit Island in the lagoon. Large scale collapse of the summit area of the volcano produced a caldera which was filled rapidly by lavas of the Mount Lidgbird Basalt some 6.4 Ma ago, bringing to a close the volcanic history of Lord Howe Island. The shield volcano thus was built during a short interval in the late Miocene. Palaeomagnetic data show that the North Ridge Basalt and the Mount Lidgbird Basalt were erupted during periods when the geomagnetic field had normal polarity, and that their formation was separated by at least one interval of reversed polarity when the dykes and cone sheets were emplaced. The directions of magnetisation for the lavas and intrusives are such that, palaeomagnetically, no movement of Lord Howe Island is detected since its formation. Lord Howe Island is the subaerial part of a large seamount which lies at the southern end of a northerly-trending line of volcanic seamounts extending for more than 1000 km. The Lord Howe seamount chain probably was produced by movement of the Australian lithospheric plate over a magma source or hot spot located below the plate within the upper mantle. O

Tholeiitic lavas of the North Ridge Basalt comprise the main shield building phase and were erupted about 6.9 Ma ago. The Boat Harbour Breccia probably formed within the throat of the volcano and, together with the North Ridge Basalt, is intruded by numerous basaltic dykes, which grade into a cone sheet complex near the main vent. Large scale collapse of the summit area of the volcano produced a caldera which was filled rapidly by lavas of the Mount Lidgbird Basalt some 6.4 Ma ago, bringing to a close the volcanic history of Lord Howe Island. ABSTRACT The age of formation of the Lapstone Monocline has been long considered to be late Pliocene/early Pleistocene (the Kosciusko Uplift) but it is now generally thought to be much older. Palaeomagnetic data from haematite-rich beds within the Hawkesbury Sandstone on and about the monocline indicate that it formed before the oldest haematite was introduced to these beds. The age of this oldest haematite is 15 ± 7 Ma. On the basis of these data, the age of the monocline is unlikely to be less than 8 Ma, probably exceeds 15 Ma, and could be older than 22 Ma. Traditional interpretations of the Blue Mountains portion of the southeastern Australian highland and the Lapstone Monocline, placed uplift/folding in the late Pliocene/early Pleistocene, during the Kosciusko Uplift (or Kosciusko Stage). This age of folding—• first suggested by Andrews (1910, 1934) and re- iterated by many others, including Browne (1969) and Scheibner (1976)—was based on a Davisian interpretation of eastern Australian landforms. Osborne (1948) suggested that the fold may be con- siderably older, but only more recently, with the advent of the K-Ar isotopic dating method and the determination of the physical ages of many basalts throughout eastern Australia, has there been any real emphasis on the antiquity of the southeastern Aus- tralian highland. By comparing components of stable magnetization measured in oriented samples of the dykes with the catalogue of palaeomagnetic data for late Precambrian and early Palaeozoic rock sequences and units obtained from independent studies, it is possible to place constraints on the age of dolerite intrusion. This strategy of using palaeomagnetism as an indirect dating technique is most successful where a detailed record of apparent polar wander (APW) is available. For the particular time span under consideration, studies by McWilliams and McElhinny (1980), Kirschvink (1978), Klootwijk (1980), Embleton and Giddings (1974) and Goleby (1980) have provided the necessary detail. PALAEOMAGNETIC RESULTS Fifty-one independently oriented samples from nine dykes were collected using a portable field drill. The sampling sites are shown in Fig. 1. The measurement of magnetic remanence was accomplished using a DIGICO complete results fluxgate magnetometer. Experiments to test the stability of remanence to alternating field (AF) demagnetization as a measure of the coercive force spectra were carried out with a SCHONSTEDT GSD-1 demagnetizer, screened from the Earth's magnetic field with /x-metal, and with a custom built three-axis AF demagnetizer housed in specially constructed field coils similar to those described by McElhinny et al (1970). Partial thermal demagnetisation to measure the blocking temperature spectra was carried out in a large, non- magnetic furnace again screened from the influence of the Earth's magnetic field with a custom built ten-coil field control system. Schmidt CSIRO Division of Mineral Physics and Mineralogy, PO Box 136, North Ryde, NSW 2113, Australia. Samples from nine dolerite dykes that outcrop in the Northampton Block, Western Australia, have been analysed to investigate the palaeomagnetic constraints that may be placed on the timing of magmatic events in relation to the widespread lead and zinc mineralization in the Northampton Mineral Field. The palaeomagnetic directions are consistent with a group of pole positions obtained from independent studies of formations of latest Precambrian and very earliest Cambrian age. The pole for the dykes lies at latitude 47.1°S, longitude 317.3°E (A95=7.9°). A comparison with the palaeomagnetic catalogue suggests that the dykes cannot be younger. Results from radiometric studies yield ages for two dykes at 550 Ma and a third dyke at 750 Ma. The results indicate that the dykes were intruded considerably earlier than the mineralization age (late- Early to early-Mid Paleozoic) and hence cast doubt on the role of the intrusive event as either the source of mineralization or the principal catalyst for the mobilization of pre-existing mineral deposits. Located in the Little Ajo Mountains of western Pima county (Fig. 1), the deposit at Ajo is typical of the province in its association with a Late Cretaceous-early Tertiary (Laramide) intrusion. The intrusion is relatively iso- lated from other mineralized plutons in the region and lies within a wide area of mid-Tertiary volcanics. The intrusion at Ajo is hosted by a thick sequence of volcanic rocks, and the associated orebody is similar to the porphyry copper-gold-type deposit of the Lone Star mining district in Graham county, Arizona, de- scribed by Langton and Williams (1982). One of the first copper districts to be mined by Americans after the Gadsden Purchase of 1853, the deposit at Ajo has produced approximately 2.5 million tons of copper, with gold and molybdenum by-products, between 1917 and 1984 when production was suspended. The first comprehensive study of the geologic framework of the Ajo mining district was that of Gil- luly (1946). He concluded that the orebody is asso- ciated with the displaced apex of a large pluton ex- posed by deeper erosion to the west. Detailed grid mapping of this large pluton by Wadsworth (1968) made possible its subdivision into multiple intrusive phases an

ossible its subdivision into multiple intrusive phases and showed petrologic similarities between a portion of the pluton and the ore zone, supporting Gilluly's interpretation. K-Ar ages of 63 to 65 m.y. (McDowell, 1971) confirmed the Laramide age of the mineralized rocks but indicated an age of approxi- mately 20 m.y. for the pluton to the west (Table 1). This discrepancy was ascribed by McDowell (1971) to a younger episode of alteration in the western plu- ton. Cox et al. (1981) described highly saline fluid inclusions in igneous quartz grains from the western pluton which also contain chalcopyrite daughter min- erals. This reinforced the hypothesis that hydrother- mal fluids had evolved from the crystallizing pluton and formed the porphyry copper deposit now faulted down to the east. Cox and Ohta (1984) remapped the pluton, revising Wadsworth's (1968) work, and noted sodic-calcic alteration assemblages like those recog- nized in the deep zones of the Yerington porphyry copper deposit in Nevada (Carten, 1979). carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: the porphyry copper province centered in southeastern Arizona. Located in the Little Ajo Mountains of western Pima county (Fig. 1), the deposit at Ajo is typical of the province in its association with a Late Cretaceous-early Tertiary (Laramide) intrusion. The intrusion is relatively iso- lated from other mineralized plutons in the region and lies within a wide area of mid-Tertiary volcanics. The intrusion at Ajo is hosted by a thick sequence of volcanic rocks, and the associated orebody is similar to the porphyry copper-gold-type deposit of the Lone Star mining district in Graham county, Arizona, de- scribed by Langton and Williams (1982). One of the first copper districts to be mined by Americans after the Gadsden Purchase of 1853, the deposit at Ajo has produced approximately 2.5 million tons of copper, with gold and molybdenum by-products, between 1917 and 1984 when production was suspended. The first comprehensive study of the geologic framework of the Ajo mining district was that of Gil- luly (1946). He concluded that the orebody is asso- ciated with the displaced apex of a large pluton ex- posed by deeper erosion to the west. Detailed grid mapping of this large pluton by Wadsworth (1968) made possible its subdivision into multiple intrusive phases an

ossible its subdivision into multiple intrusive phases and showed petrologic similarities between a portion of the pluton and the ore zone, supporting Gilluly's interpretation. K-Ar ages of 63 to 65 m.y. (McDowell, 1971) confirmed the Laramide age of the mineralized rocks but indicated an age of approxi- mately 20 m.y. for the pluton to the west (Table 1). This discrepancy was ascribed by McDowell (1971) to a younger episode of alteration in the western plu- ton. Cox et al. (1981) described highly saline fluid inclusions in igneous quartz grains from the western pluton which also contain chalcopyrite daughter min- erals. This reinforced the hypothesis that hydrother- mal fluids had evolved from the crystallizing pluton and formed the porphyry copper deposit now faulted down to the east. Cox and Ohta (1984) remapped the pluton, revising Wadsworth's (1968) work, and noted sodic-calcic alteration assemblages like those recog- nized in the deep zones of the Yerington porphyry copper deposit in Nevada (Carten, 1979). This ob- servation also supported a cogenetic relationship be- tween the pluton and the orebody. However, this re- lationship recently has been put in doubt by unpub- lished U-Pb data (L. T. Silver, oral commun., 1983; J. S. Stacey andJ. L. Wooden, wri

The K-Ar geochro- nology was undertaken to test the hypothesis that the western pluton and the eastern mineralized intrusion are cogenetic. Because intrusive rocks lack conven- tional indicators of the palcohorizontal, palcomag- netic measurements were made on samples from plu- tonic and related igneous rocks of the Ajo mining dis- trict to estimte the structural disturbance these rocks have undergone since emplacement. Upon cooling below their magnetic blocking temperatures, igneous rocks acquire a remanent magnetization parallel to the ambient geomagnetic field that is stable over geo- logic time. Stable remanent magnetizations may also be acquired by rocks subject to subblocking-temper- ature chemical alteration. The direction of the geo- magnetic field at Ajo for the time the plutonic and related igneous rocks cooled and became magnetic can be calculated from palcomagnetic directions for contemporaneous rocks at undisturbed sites else- where in North America. Thus, comparisons of pa- lcomagnetic directions from igneous rocks in the Ajo district with the expected Late Cretaceous-early Ter- tiary and middle Tertiary geomagnetic-field directions provide initial postcooling horizontal datums for these rock units. The paleomagnetic data ob- tained from such cores consist of a set of inclination values of known sequence but unknown spacing in time. The objective in analyzing these data is to determine the paleolatitude of the sampling site. If paleomagnetic data are available from widely separated sites on the same plate and if both the paleolatitude and its associated confidence limits are known for each site, the data may be combined to yield a paleopole for the plate and an ellipse of 95% confidence [Gordon and Cox, 1980]. The coordinates of the paleopole and the orientation, size, and ellipticity of the confidence ellipse depend not only on the site coordi- nates and paleocolatitudes but also on the magnitude of the confidence intervals. Therefore the need has arisen for a method of analysis that yields an accurate estimate of confidence limits for paleolatitude data from azimuthally unoriented vertical cores. Rather than a succession of central volcanic activities with only one or two centres being active at any one time (as depicted by Grunevald), parallel development of a number of centres is indicated. Rather than an island-wide basement being established early on, it now appears that the exposed basement to each centre is not significantly older than much of the superstructure. Thus there are areas of basement, previously regarded as Eocene, which now appear to be Plio- Pleistocene. Moreover, some longer-range lateral correlations on the basis of petrographic type are now seen to be invalid. The results will be discussed regionally and generally in order of increasing age, though this is not practicable in every case. The active centre of Mt Pelee, designated Quaternary by Grunevald has only a single whole rock age determination of 0.4 + 0.2 Ma (Andreieff et al. 1976). Volcanics of the Piton Mont Conil area have yielded a whole rock age of 0.6 Ma from a plagioclase-phyric andesite (Nagle et al. 1976) and 2.63 Ma from a hornblende separate. Marine geological studies of the Venezuelan Basin indicate that it has been an area of pelagic deposition since a period of extensive flood basalt emission about 80 Ma ago (Donnelly 1975). The Greater Antilles have a stratigraphic history extending well back into the Mesozoic (Khudoley & Meyerhofs 1971). Fossil identifications on the islands of the Lesser Antilles indicate ages of marine sediments as old as early Eocene (Lewis & Robinson 1976). These early Tertiary sediments were deposited on a developing island arc where activity has since ceased, and has been succeeded as the site of volcanism by the Volcanic Caribbees. The respective sedimentary sequences are Pre- or Early-Devonian, Devonian, Permo-Triassic and Triassic. The representative samples were tested for NRM stability against AF and thermal demagnetization, ARM and TRM acquisi­ tion, and AF demagnetization of ARM. The following results were obtained. Introduction Paleo magnetic investigations of the Beacon Group were carried out with the samples collected from the Ferrar Glacier (78°S, 161 °E) by TURNBULL (1959), and from the Wright and Victoria Valleys (77.5°S, l6I.0°E) by BULL et al. (1962). They reached the general conclusion that NRM (Natural Remanent Magnetization) at these sites is parallel to that of indubitably younger dolerite sills (Ferrar dolerite) in spite of a separation of 150 m from the lower boundary of the sill. That is, a large intrusive mass of the Ferrar dolerite nearby caused sufficient heating to raise the Beacon Group to the Curie point and must have been remagnetized in alignment with the ambient geomagnetic field in the Jurassic Age. According to the geological evidence in East Antarctica, the formations ranging in age from Middle Paleozoic to Messozoic were only the Beacon Group (sandstone) in the Transantarctic Mountains and the Prince Charles Mountains of the Lambert Glacier (i.e. RA VICH and FEDOROV, 1977). Therefore, it is very important to carry out an investiga­ tion of the Beacon Group paleomagnetically in order to elucidate the history of Gond­ wanaland, as the East Antarctic plate is probably situated in the center of that region. 2. No results were obtained from the Lower Permian Qixia Formation limestones or the (Lower)- Upper Permian Maokou Formation limestones.
